```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

The course coordinator wants to know whether participants were satisfied, and
whether the two centres tell the same story. Start with a frequency table,
then choose the layout that answers each follow-up question. Results remain
ordinary tables that work with dplyr.

## Start with one question

These are the same twelve participants used in
[Getting started](getting-started.html), keeping only the columns needed here.

```{r survey, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",
    3, "Riverside", "No",
    4, "Riverside", NA,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
   12, "Hilltop",   NA
)

survey |> tab(satisfied)
```

Seven participants said yes, three said no, and two did not answer. Read the
columns in terms of the question you want to answer:

| Column | Question |
|--------|----------|
| `n` | How many participants gave this answer? |
| `percent` | What percentage of **all twelve** participants is that? |
| `valid` | What percentage of the **ten who answered** is that? |
| `cum`, `valid_cum` | What percentage have we reached in the displayed order? |

All four percentage columns use a 0-100 scale. Thus the yes share is 58.3%
of everyone and 70% of respondents. Missing categories have no valid percentage.
Cumulative percentages are most useful for categories with a meaningful order.

## Choose joint, separate or cross-tabulated counts

The three `tab` functions answer different questions using the same columns.

### Which combinations occur?

`tab()` counts combinations in one long table. With two columns, each row
is a centre-answer combination:

```{r joint}
survey |> tab(centre, satisfied)
```

Here `percent` and `cum` use all twelve participants; `valid` and `valid_cum`
use the ten with both centre and satisfaction observed. Adding a third variable
would count three-way combinations.

### What is each variable's distribution?

`tab1()` makes separate one-way tables. Use `.type = "tibble"` to stack them
into one table with a `variable` column:

```{r separate}
survey |> tab1(centre, satisfied, .type = "tibble")
```

Each variable has its own denominator. The default instead returns a named
list, convenient when the tables will be used separately.

### How do the centres compare side by side?

`tab2()` puts the second variable's categories in columns. Cells contain
counts, rather than the percentages from `tab()`:

```{r cross}
survey |> tab2(centre, satisfied)
```

With more than two selected variables, `tab2()` returns a list of tables for
every pair, rather than one higher-dimensional table. Use `.flip = TRUE`
to exchange rows and columns.

## Compare percentages within each centre

To compare satisfaction rates, put the centre in `.by` instead of counting
it as another measured variable:

```{r within-centres}
survey |> tab(satisfied, .by = centre)
```

Both centres have six participants and five observed answers. Riverside's
yes share is 80% of respondents; Hilltop's is 60%. The missing answers still
appear, so the difference between all-participant and valid shares stays visible.

One-way and joint tables also inherit `group_by()` groups:

```{r inherited-groups}
survey |>
  group_by(centre) |>
  tab(satisfied) |>
  filter(satisfied == "Yes") |>
  select(centre, n, percent, valid)
```

The result is ungrouped. An explicit `.by` replaces inherited groups.
`tab2()` and `fre2()` require an explicit `.by` to make separate cross-tables
by group; `group_by()` alone does not split their results.

## Add totals and readable labels

`fre()` adds total rows. Here we encode the answer to illustrate imported
numeric categories with value labels:

```{r labelled-totals}
labelled <- survey |> mutate(answer_code = encode(satisfied))

labelled |> fre(answer_code)
```

`tab()` retains stored category codes and types; `fre()` displays value labels.
Distinct codes remain distinct even when they share a label. `fre1()` adds
totals to separate one-way tables; `fre2()` adds row and column totals to a
cross-tabulation:

```{r cross-totals}
survey |> fre2(centre, satisfied)
```

`fre2()` displays labels for row categories; column headers retain category
codes. You can also request totals with `.total = TRUE` in the `tab` family.
Totals are useful for presentation, but use tables without total rows for
further arithmetic so observations are not counted twice.

## Order and reuse the results

Which answer is most common? `.desc = TRUE` sorts by decreasing count,
keeping missing values last:

```{r frequency-order}
survey |> tab(satisfied, .desc = TRUE)
```

Factors follow their level order by default; other categories sort by value.
`.group_order = "frequency"` separately orders group blocks by their totals.
Use dplyr to keep the categories relevant to a report:

```{r reuse}
survey |>
  tab(satisfied, .by = centre) |>
  filter(!is.na(satisfied)) |>
  arrange(centre, desc(n)) |>
  select(centre, satisfied, n, valid)
```

Filtering here keeps the percentages already calculated. To change a
denominator, filter the source observations **before** calling `tab()`.
Empty strings count as observed answers, so clean blank text first if it
means nonresponse.

## Count a file that already contains frequencies

Suppose a second coordinator sends an aggregate file: one row represents
several people. Use the frequency column as `.wt`:

```{r weights}
register <- tribble(
  ~satisfied, ~people,
  "Yes",           7,
  "No",            3,
  NA,              2
)

register |> tab(satisfied, .wt = people)
```

This reproduces the individual-level table. Frequency weights sum to the
reported counts. Analytic weights (`.wt_type = "analytic"`) instead rescale
weights within each group to its number of rows; their percentages agree,
but their counts have a different interpretation. Missing weights exclude
rows, and negative weights are invalid. These options do not account for a
complex survey design.

## Association tests and longer tables

For an association test, `.chi2 = TRUE` adds Pearson's chi-square and Cramer's V.
Remove missing answers first when nonresponse should not enter the test:

```{r association}
association <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(satisfied)) |>
  tab2(centre, satisfied, .chi2 = TRUE)
```

The test is reported as a message. Its numerical results are also available
on the returned table:

```{r association-results}
attr(association, "chi2")
```

This tiny teaching sample has small expected cell counts, so use the example
to learn the interface, rather than draw an inference about the programme.
Analytic weights are not supported for this test.

Score variables can produce long tables because every distinct value is
counted. Add the first assessment item from our survey and shorten its display
with a one-time printer, which still returns every row:

```{r long-table}
survey |>
  mutate(score = c(2, 4, NA, 6, 8, 4, 3, 5, 7, 9, NA, 6)) |>
  tab(score) |>
  print_interval(n = 6)
```

For formatted reports, the `fre` family supports `.type = "flextable"` when
that optional package is installed. See the
[output conventions](containers-and-missing-values.html) for lists and table
classes, or continue to [measurement summaries](summary-statistics.html).
